newsitem.title: USA: Next downstream move for U.S. major may be Europe.
newsitem.headline: Next downstream move for U.S. major may be Europe.

text.p: After a spate of big deals in the U.S., the next downstream alliance for a domestic oil major is likely to be in Europe and may involve Texaco Inc and France's Total SA.
Analysts say that in February, Texaco chief executive Peter Bijur told them the company would complete a study in 90 days on its European options, and that time is now up.
"When I talked to them a few days ago, they said nothing had been decided, but after the BP and Mobil success, it is just a question of time," said one New York-based analyst.
British Petroleum Co Plc and Mobil Corp in January said the benefits from their European downstream venture would exceed forecasts of $400-$500 million pretax.
A spokesman for Texaco said that there were no specific partners under consideration at the moment, but added that the company was looking hard at its European downstream.
U.S. downstream return on capital is in single digits, in Europe, it is bedevilled by retail wars in Britain and France.
Texaco's international downstream division operating earnings fell to $252 million in 1996, compared with $358 million in 1995, due mainly to weakness in the UK market.
Analysts say Texaco believes it is big enough not to have to form a downstream venture with another U.S. major such as Exxon Corp or Texaco's existing U.S. downstream partner Royal Dutch/Shell.
And BP is off-limits because of its deal with Mobil.
"Among the European majors, that leaves France's Total SA or Elf Aquitaine, with Total the more likely," said one New York-based oil analyst.
Further credence is being given to a Total deal by traders of the French oil giant's American Depositary Receipts.
"We hear Total may announce a restrucuring as early as this week," said one ADR trader, who noted the company had not announced anything at its shareholder meeting today.
Texaco owns one refinery in Europe, a 180,000 barrels per day plant in the UK and has 35 percent stake in another.
Its petroleum product sales in 1996 were 461,000 barrels per day, according to the company's earnings release.
Analysts estimate Texaco has a seven percent share of the UK retail market and a somewhat smaller share in Europe.
European analysts say that one possible trend in Europe is a series of smaller alliances.
"People may be looking at deals on a regional basis, although something people have talked about is a possible link-up between Elf and Total," said Greg Quine, analyst at JP Morgan in London.
He noted that Elf had gotten off to a slower start in restructuring and there may be competition issues.
Elf already has a UK downstream venture Chevron Corp of the U.S.
This deal will actually result in the much needed closure of European refining capacity at Chevron's Gulf Oil unit.
However, big closures as a result of mergers are as unlikely in Europe as they are here because companies face charges, environmental costs and lose positive cashflow.
Total chairman Thierry Desmarest has said he would like to see a deal based on cutting refining capacity in Europe, but analysts are sceptical that this will happen.
Instead Desmarest is paring capital spending on refineries to the bone and the company has slashed its French retail sites by 10.8 percent between 1993 and 1995 to some 3,300.

"The industry here is very tight and the base position is that everyone is talking to everyone else in Europe as in the U.S.," said JP Morgan's Quine. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
